terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build Kasimir's bench here and run it, once main makes a caddy or two.

tasks.title: Write the class template
nextSteps: Write the template line, then the class with its two private members.
Write the constructor, with the limit in its member initialiser list.
Declare `at` in the class, and make a `Caddy<int>` in `main` to try it.
hints: A class template is a class written once with its type left open, exactly as a function template is. Everything inside the class can use `T`.

`add` asks first whether the caddy is full, by comparing how many items it holds with its limit. A type with nothing but copies can still go into a `std::vector`, as long as nothing asks the vector to make one from nothing.

The shape is `template <typename T> class Caddy { private: std::vector<T> items; int limit; public: Caddy(int most) : limit(most) {} bool add(const T& item) { ... } int count() const { ... } const T& at(int place) const; };`.

tasks.title: Reach an item by its place, below the class
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2` in `src/caddy.h`, below the class, write the body of `at`: it gives back the item at that place, counted from 0, as a reference to a `const T`. When there is no item at that place, below 0 or from `count()` on, it throws a `std::out_of_range`.

Check builds this task with a `Caddy` of its own in place of your class, written as Task 1 asks, and your body of `at` below it, in a program of its own that includes `caddy.h`. It reads items of a `Caddy<int>` and of a caddy of its own type by their place, and asks for places where there is no item.
nextSteps: Below the class, write the template line again.
Write the first line of `at` as a member of `Caddy<T>`, matching its declaration, `const` at the end included.
Throw a `std::out_of_range` when the place has no item.
Otherwise give back the item there, and print one from `main`.
hints: Outside the class, `at` is written with the class in front of its name, as in part 5. Here the class is `Caddy<T>`, and `T` means nothing below the class until a template line says it is a type.
Places go from 0 to one less than `count()`. A place below 0 is no place either.
The shape is `template <typename T> const T& Caddy<T>::at(int place) const { if (place < 0 || place >= count()) { throw std::out_of_range("no item there"); } return items[place]; }`.

tasks.title: Fill the shelf caddy with repairs
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3` in `src/main.cpp`, write a function called `fillCaddy` that takes the repairs as a reference to a `const std::vector<Repair>` and a limit as an `int`. It makes a caddy of repairs with that limit, adds the repairs to it in order with `add`, and gives the caddy back. Repairs that do not fit are left out.

Check builds your `main.cpp` with a `caddy.h` of its own in place of yours, written as Tasks 1 and 2 ask, that counts calls to `add`. It calls `fillCaddy` with repairs and limits of its own, an empty list and a limit of 0 included, and reads the tickets of what the caddy holds.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const std::vector<Repair>&` and an `int` in, a caddy of repairs back.
Make the caddy with the limit.
Add each repair in order with `add`.
Give the caddy back, and print its tickets from `main` with `count` and `at`.
hints: `Caddy` alone is not a type. A caddy of repairs is a class of its own, made from the template by naming `Repair` in the angle brackets.
`add` already keeps the limit, so the loop can hand it every repair and let it refuse the ones that do not fit.
The shape is `Caddy<Repair> fillCaddy(const std::vector<Repair>& repairs, int limit) { Caddy<Repair> caddy(limit); for (const Repair& repair : repairs) { caddy.add(repair); } return caddy; }`.
